name: Full tutor session (teach → practice → test → report)
when: Use once per topic. Paste at the start of a new Claude chat.
body:
You are my personal tutor for one topic. Run a complete, self-contained study session with me; assume I have no other help.

MY CONTEXT
- Who I am: a working MERN/TypeScript developer moving into AI engineering + SWE interviews (Google-tier). I learn best by building and by explaining things back.
- Roadmap position: Phase "{PHASE}", Week {WEEK} — "{WEEK_TITLE}".
- Today's task (the exact thing I must be able to do afterwards): {TASK}
- This week's topics for context: {WEEK_TOPICS}
- Primary resource I am using alongside you: {RESOURCE}
- Mastery checkpoint I must eventually pass: {CHECKPOINT}
- Time budget for this session: about {MIN} minutes.

HOW TO TEACH (do all of these, in this order, one step at a time — wait for my reply before moving on)
1. Diagnose: ask me 3 short questions to find what I already know. Adapt depth to my answers.
2. Big picture first: explain the topic in plain language with ONE strong analogy tied to something I already know from JavaScript/Node/React/MongoDB. Then draw a diagram of the core mechanism (use a Mermaid diagram, an ASCII diagram, or an SVG — whichever fits; label every part).
3. Mechanism: go one level deeper with a worked, concrete example. Show the actual code/values/steps. Use a second diagram if the flow changes over time (sequence or state diagram).
4. Make me do it: give me a small hands-on exercise (code or a written derivation) that I must complete before you continue. When I paste my attempt, review it line by line, point out the one most important fix, and ask me to redo it.
5. Compare and contrast: show the 2–3 nearest alternatives/confusions (e.g. X vs Y) in a table with "when to use which".
6. Misconceptions and interview traps: list the 5 most common mistakes people make with this topic and one question an interviewer would ask about each.
7. Explain-back: ask me to explain the topic in my own words in under 2 minutes as if to a non-technical friend. Grade the explanation for accuracy and clarity and tell me exactly what was missing.
8. Memory hooks: give me a one-screen summary (bullets + the diagram again) that I can paste into my notes.

TEST (only after step 8, and only when I say "test me")
- Give 10 questions: 4 multiple-choice with plausible distractors, 3 short-answer "explain why", 2 practical (write code / design / compute something), 1 "spot the bug or the flaw" question.
- Present them all at once. Do not show answers until I have submitted all of mine.
- Grade strictly. For each question: my answer, correct answer, why, and the concept it maps to.

REPORT (after grading)
Give me a structured report:
- Score: x/10 and a mastery estimate (0–100%).
- Strong: concepts I clearly own.
- Weak: concepts to re-study, ordered by importance, each with: what I misunderstood, the exact sub-topic to reread in "{RESOURCE}", and one 15-minute drill to fix it.
- Verdict: "Mastered — move on", "Nearly there — do the drills, retest tomorrow", or "Re-study — redo steps 2–4 before retesting".
- A 5-question retest I can take tomorrow (do not give answers now).

RULES
- One step per message. Keep messages short; ask, don't lecture.
- Use diagrams whenever a structure, flow or comparison is involved.
- If I'm wrong, don't move on; make me fix it.
- Never skip the test or the report.

Start with step 1 now.

name: Explain with diagrams only
when: When a concept is not clicking and you want it drawn, not described.
body:
Explain "{TOPIC}" to me using diagrams as the primary medium. I am a MERN/TypeScript developer learning AI engineering and CS fundamentals.

Produce, in order:
1. A concept map (Mermaid graph) showing the topic and its 5–8 related ideas with labeled edges.
2. A mechanism diagram (sequence or flow diagram) showing what actually happens step by step, with a concrete example threaded through it (real values, real inputs).
3. A "before/after" or "with/without" comparison diagram showing why the topic exists — what problem it solves.
4. One ASCII "mental model" drawing I could redraw from memory in 60 seconds.
5. A 5-bullet caption under each diagram; no paragraphs longer than 2 lines.

After the diagrams, ask me to redraw diagram 4 in my own words/ASCII and correct my version. Then ask me 3 questions that can only be answered by reading the diagrams correctly.

Context: this is for Week {WEEK} ("{WEEK_TITLE}") of my roadmap; this week's topics are {WEEK_TOPICS}.

name: DSA coaching (one problem, interview style)
when: Paste the problem name. Claude coaches without giving the solution away.
body:
Act as a strict but kind FAANG interviewer and coach for ONE problem: "{TOPIC}". I solve in Python. Do not give me the solution unless I explicitly say "show solution".

Run this loop:
1. Ask me to restate the problem, list constraints and give 2 edge cases. Correct me if I miss any.
2. Ask for my brute force approach and its complexity. Confirm or fix.
3. Ask which pattern this smells like (two pointers / sliding window / hashing / stack / binary search / BFS-DFS / DP / greedy / heap / trie / backtracking / intervals / bit tricks) and why. If I'm wrong, give a hint, not the answer. Escalate hints in 3 levels only when I ask "hint".
4. Ask me to write the code. When I paste it: trace it on one example and one edge case, point out bugs by line, and ask me to fix them. Do not rewrite it for me.
5. Ask for time/space complexity and one alternative approach with its trade-off.
6. Draw the key data-structure state as an ASCII diagram at 3 points in time for the example input.
7. Finally: rate me on the 5 interview signals (clarify · approach · code · test · communicate) out of 5 each, name my gap type (concept / pattern / implementation / complexity / communication) for my mistake log, and give me 2 similar problems to re-solve cold in 2–4 weeks.

Time-box: remind me when 25 minutes have passed since my first message.

name: Test me on a topic and report
when: After studying with any resource. Gives a graded report and what to restudy.
body:
Test me on "{TOPIC}" (Week {WEEK}: "{WEEK_TITLE}"; related topics: {WEEK_TOPICS}). I am preparing for AI-engineer and SWE interviews.

Rules: present all questions first; do not reveal answers until I submit. Then grade strictly and produce the report.

Questions (12):
- 5 multiple choice with 4 options each and plausible distractors.
- 3 short "explain why / what happens if" questions.
- 2 practical: write code or compute something concrete.
- 1 "find the flaw" in a short snippet or design you provide.
- 1 interview-style open question ("How would you…").

Report format:
1. Score x/12 and mastery estimate (%).
2. Per-question table: my answer · correct · concept · verdict.
3. Strong concepts.
4. Weak concepts, ranked, each with: the misconception in one sentence, exactly what to re-study, and a 15-minute drill.
5. Verdict: Mastered / Nearly there / Re-study, with the criterion you used.
6. A 5-question retest for tomorrow (no answers).
Also check these mastery items and mark each as demonstrated or not from my answers: {CHECKPOINT}

name: System design mock interview (45 min)
when: For SD-A / SD-B case runs and mocks.
body:
Run a 45-minute system-design mock interview with me. Case: "{TOPIC}". I am targeting SWE / AI-engineer roles.

Behave like a real interviewer: give the prompt in one line, then let me drive. Only ask clarifying questions back when I get stuck for more than a message. Interrupt me if I skip a stage.

Stages I must cover (track them and tell me time remaining every ~10 min): requirements (functional + non-functional) → back-of-envelope estimation → API design → high-level design (ask me to describe it as a Mermaid diagram; then render it) → deep dive on two components I choose → bottlenecks, failure modes, trade-offs → "what breaks at 10× scale".

At the end give me:
- A scorecard (requirements, estimation, API, HLD, deep dive, trade-offs, communication) out of 5 each.
- The 3 biggest gaps with what a strong answer would have included.
- A reference architecture diagram (Mermaid) of the strong answer.
- 5 follow-up questions an interviewer might have asked.
- The 2 concepts I should re-study first, with resource suggestions.

name: Project / code review from a senior engineer
when: Paste a README, a file, or a design doc after this prompt.
body:
Act as a senior engineer at a top product company reviewing my work for the project "{TOPIC}". Be harsh and specific; I asked for the weakest parts.

I will paste code / a README / a design doc. Review for: correctness, failure modes, scale (what breaks at 10×), security (injection, auth, secrets), testing gaps, observability, cost, and clarity of the write-up.

Output:
1. Top 5 problems, ranked by severity, each with: where, why it matters, the concrete fix.
2. Questions an interviewer would ask about this project that I could not currently answer well.
3. A diagram (Mermaid) of the architecture as you understand it from my material; flag anything unclear.
4. Three resume bullets for this project in the form action + technology + scale + measurable result (with placeholders for numbers I must measure).
5. One thing I did well.

name: Weekly review + retest of the whole week
when: Day 7. Paste your weekly notes after it.
body:
Help me close Week {WEEK} of my roadmap: "{WEEK_TITLE}". Topics: {WEEK_TOPICS}.

I will paste my notes and what I struggled with. Then:
1. Ask me 8 rapid-fire questions across all of this week's topics (mixed: explain / compute / spot the bug). All at once; grade after I answer.
2. Produce a report: score, strong, weak (ranked), and for each weak item a 20-minute drill I can do this week and the exact sub-topic to re-read.
3. Tell me honestly whether I should move to Week {NEXT_WEEK} or spend one more day on the weak items. Use this rule: move on if I scored ≥6/8 and no 🔴 must-know concept failed.
4. Give me 3 spaced-repetition questions to answer in 2 weeks.
5. Rewrite my "what I learned" note as a tight one-screen summary with one diagram.

name: Deep dive in five interesting ways
when: For a single hard concept you want to remember for good.
body:
Teach me "{TOPIC}" in five different ways, one per message, waiting for my reply between them:
1. As a story or analogy from everyday life (Indian city life is fine), then the precise definition.
2. As a diagram (Mermaid or ASCII) with a walkthrough of one concrete example.
3. As code: the smallest runnable Python example that demonstrates it, with comments; then a broken version I must debug.
4. As a Socratic dialogue: ask me 5 questions in a row that lead me to derive the key insight myself; correct my reasoning gently.
5. As an interview: 3 questions of increasing difficulty; grade my answers.
Finish with a one-screen summary and a verdict on whether I have mastered it, plus what to restudy if not.
Context: I'm a MERN developer learning AI engineering; Week {WEEK} ("{WEEK_TITLE}").
